item.title: What DevOps Taught Me About Managing ADHD, Attention and Flow
item.description:
I was chatting recently with someone else who has ADHD about how I manage notes, tasks and to-dos. What surprised me was that the useful bit wasn’t really the tools. It was the process I’d gone through to get there.

I was diagnosed with ADHD relatively recently, and that gave me a useful lens for understanding why some of my productivity systems had worked for a while and then gradually collapsed under their own weight. I don’t want to dwell on the diagnosis itself here. What mattered was the reframing.

item.title: The Unicorn Project
item.description: I’ve had the privilege to get early access to The Unicorn Project by Gene Kim. Set within Parts Unlimited a large manufacturing and retail organisation that is struggling to come to terms with software as a first class citizen. Yes for those of you who have read The Phoenix Project this story is set in the same organisation and you see many of the same characters and events that occurred. In fact this tale follows another character within the narrative that was only briefly introduced before, namely a developer.

item.title: An Example of Flow
item.description: I’ve been reading The Goal as well as The Phoenix Project. Whilst there are many important principals in these novels and I highly recommend them. I wanted to highlight one in particular. The danger of too much Inventory or unfinished work. Recently I was working on an Agile project. This team conformed to the scrum framework zealously, the application architecture was solid, the team were beyond excellent, we had fantastic and driven product owner. Yet despite all of this we consistently missed our sprint goal. Each retrospective we looked at the process adjusted and tried again. We reduced sprint lengths reduced the number of stories in a sprint, inflated our estimates for the stories, and quite a number of other adjustments, nothing seemed to resolve the issue. We were confounded nothing seemed to resolve what was happening. Finally Matt the Scrum Master suggest one last thing.
